questions.prompt: The MIDI keyboard's activity indicator blinks, yet the project stays silent and nothing appears in the piano roll.
questions.answer: The recording filter is not set to record note data
questions.distractor: The keyboard is transmitting audio that the piano roll cannot display
questions.correction: The indicator proves that data is arriving. Note data is stored only when the recording filter includes it, and MIDI never carries audio, so a display problem cannot be caused by an audio signal.

questions.prompt: In a recorded guitar take a single loud strum is distorted while the quieter playing is clean.
questions.answer: Reduce the record level feeding the armed track, then record the take again
questions.distractor: Lower the headphone volume and export the project again
questions.correction: The overload happened before the monitoring stage, so the stored samples are already clipped. Exporting again reproduces the same damaged file, whereas a correct input level prevents the problem at its source.

questions.prompt: A rhythm part that should push slightly ahead of the beat sounds lifeless after full-strength quantisation to a straight grid.
questions.answer: Keep the original and compare it with a lower-strength or groove-template version that matches the played feel
questions.distractor: Quantise the same part again with identical settings to remove the remaining deviation
questions.correction: Full strength removed the intended anticipation along with accidental drift. Partial strength and templates are designed to mix original and template positions, and preserving the source makes the comparison possible.

questions.prompt: Two parts sound clearly separated in stereo, but the pad covers the guitar as soon as the mix is heard in mono.
questions.answer: Panning separated them only in stereo, so their registers or densities must be changed
questions.distractor: Pan the two parts further apart until the mono version also improves
questions.correction: Panning collapses when the channels are combined, so overlapping frequency content returns. Register, voicing, and rhythmic role are the changes that survive a mono listen, with level and equalisation used afterwards.

questions.prompt: A section of the arrangement should feel fuller on every playback, without adding another instrument.
questions.answer: Draw an automation clip that moves a linked level or filter control across the section
questions.distractor: Give the section a longer name and a different clip colour
questions.correction: Automation stores a linked parameter change as editable data that repeats identically, while names and colours document form without producing any audible difference.

questions.prompt: A two-bar 4/4 pattern at 90 beats per minute begins with a dotted quarter tied to an eighth note on the same pitch. How long does that single sound last?
questions.answer: About 1.33 seconds: one beat plus one third of a beat
questions.distractor: About 1.00 second, because the tie does not add duration
questions.correction: At 90 beats per minute a beat lasts 0.667 seconds, a dotted quarter lasts 1.0 second, and the tied eighth adds 0.333 seconds, giving about 1.33 seconds for one uninterrupted sound.

questions.prompt: A recorded triad contains notes whose MIDI numbers are 60, 63, and 67. Which chord is it?
questions.answer: C minor: a minor third of three semitones with a perfect fifth
questions.distractor: C major: a major third of four semitones with a perfect fifth
questions.correction: Note 60 is C, 63 is three semitones above it, and 67 is seven semitones above it. A minor third with a perfect fifth is a minor triad, so the editor's numbers confirm the quality.

questions.prompt: A song carries a key signature of one sharp. Which note must be altered, and where does it appear on the low E string of a standard-tuned guitar?
questions.answer: F-sharp, at the second fret of the low E string
questions.distractor: F natural, at the first fret of the low E string
questions.correction: One sharp is F-sharp, which makes the key G major rather than F, and the second fret of the low E string sounds the note a semitone above the tonic's neighbour; F natural belongs to the key of C.

questions.prompt: A chart asks for I-V-vi-IV in D major. Which chords does that produce?
questions.answer: D, A, Bm, G
questions.distractor: D, G, Bm, A
questions.correction: In D major the tonic is D, the dominant is A, the sixth-degree triad is B minor, and the fourth-degree triad is G. Swapping G and A would place the subdominant where the dominant belongs, changing the progression's function.

questions.prompt: A player rehearses for two hours without a break and reports hand fatigue, having read that one survey of guitarists calculated about one practice-related injury per 2,381 hours, with failure to warm up the only variable statistically associated with higher risk.
questions.answer: Shorten sessions, add warm-ups and breaks, and reduce unnecessary grip force, seeking qualified advice if symptoms persist
questions.distractor: Extend the sessions so the hand adapts to the load
questions.correction: Load depends on force and duration, and the reported association points to preparation and pacing. The survey is a single reported dataset rather than proof that a warm-up prevents all injury, so the response is risk reduction plus qualified advice when symptoms continue.

questions.prompt: A project uses a 512-sample audio buffer at a 48 kilohertz sample rate, and playing fast parts feels sluggish. What is the approximate one-way delay, and what follows from reducing it?
questions.answer: About 10.7 milliseconds, and a smaller buffer lowers the delay while raising processor load and the risk of dropouts
questions.distractor: About 1.07 milliseconds, with no compensatory disadvantage
questions.correction: 512 divided by 48,000 is about 0.0107 seconds. The delay lives in the audio path rather than in the MIDI message, and shrinking the buffer trades latency against processing stability.

questions.prompt: While recording with a click, a player raises the headphone level because the guitar is hard to hear, then plays noticeably harder.
questions.answer: Lower the monitoring level and keep the playing effort unchanged, since monitoring does not set the recorded level
questions.distractor: Raise the record level to match the harder playing
questions.correction: Monitor level changes only what you hear, so it can be reduced freely to hear the instrument. Playing harder to compensate raises tension and clip risk, and raising the record level would move the overload point rather than the performance.

questions.prompt: Sixteenth notes at 90 beats per minute are reinterpreted with a groove template that places about sixty per cent of each pair on the first note. Roughly how long is that first note of every pair?
questions.answer: About 200 milliseconds
questions.distractor: About 133 milliseconds
questions.correction: A pair of sixteenths lasts about 333 milliseconds at this tempo; sixty per cent of that is about 200 milliseconds and the remainder is about 133 milliseconds, which is a three-to-two long-short pairing.

questions.prompt: A guitar figure becomes unclear only when a keyboard pad enters, although nothing clips and the pad is not loud. What is the least invasive first change?
questions.answer: Move one part's register or thin its voicing so the two occupy different ranges, then rebalance
questions.distractor: Boost the guitar with a limiter until it sits above the pad
questions.correction: This is masking, which is a problem of overlapping range rather than of level. Changing register or density removes the overlap; limiting only raises the guitar's level, consumes headroom, and leaves the two parts competing in the same band.

questions.prompt: An eight-bar arrangement is exported and the file is longer than the calculated body of the piece. What must be established before the file is delivered?
questions.answer: Whether the extra duration is an intended release tail or unintended silence, by listening against the section plan
questions.distractor: That the export is invalid, because a file must end precisely on the last note-off
questions.correction: Note instructions and audible tails are different things, so a reverb or instrument release can legitimately extend a file. The section plan and a listen decide whether the duration was intended, and unintended trailing silence is a revision rather than a mathematical error.

questions.prompt: A four-section sketch is planned as four bars per section at 96 beats per minute, and the second section must gain energy without a new instrument.
questions.answer: Automate a linked control across the section and confirm the change on every playback
questions.distractor: Depend on playing the section more forcefully each time it is heard
questions.correction: At 96 beats per minute a bar lasts 2.5 seconds, so each four-bar section lasts ten seconds. Automation clips store a linked parameter change as editable data that repeats identically, whereas an unrecorded performance decision cannot be reproduced or revised.

questions.prompt: A project file is sent to a collaborator; it opens, but one part is silent even though the same part plays correctly in your studio.
questions.answer: That part depends on an instrument, plugin, or external device that was not delivered, so audio should be rendered or the dependency documented
questions.distractor: MIDI files contain recorded audio, so the transferred file must be corrupted
questions.correction: Note data is instructions that require a sound source, and hardware audio must be recorded to appear in a render. Delivering a rendered audio file, or documenting the instrument and routing, prevents a correct project from arriving incomplete.
